documents.title: Low hemoglobin at work screening
documents.author: patient
documents.body:
Hi Doc,

My company did a health screening in early December. A few days later the occupational health clinic called and said my hemoglobin was a little low and my red blood cells were small. They started me on iron pills (ferrous sulfate, one a day) on December 12 and said to follow up with my own doctor. I feel completely normal. Should I get rechecked? I can ask them to send you the report.

Thanks,
Min-jun

documents.title: RE: Low hemoglobin at work screening
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Thanks for letting me know. Yes, please have occupational health fax the report to us.

I've put in a repeat blood count, iron levels and a hemoglobin electrophoresis. That last one looks for inherited hemoglobin types that make red cells small even when iron is fine. Walk in to the lab any morning; no need to fast. Keep the iron going for now. The front desk will book you for Monday 1/23 so we can go over all of it.

documents.title: First results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Min-jun — first part of your labs is back. Your blood count still shows the same mild anemia with small red cells, no better after a month of iron. Your iron level and ferritin (iron stores) are both normal, so low iron isn't what's going on. The electrophoresis usually takes about a week. We'll put it together on the 23rd.

documents.title: Occupational health screening follow-up
documents.author: occupational health
documents.body:
OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH — EMPLOYEE SCREENING SUMMARY
Employee: Min-jun Burgos  DOB 07/05/1996

documents.title: Electrophoresis back
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: The electrophoresis came back this afternoon and I think it explains everything: hemoglobin A2 is elevated and hemoglobin F is slightly up, which is the pattern of beta thalassemia trait. It's an inherited carrier state and not something dangerous. We'll talk it through Monday.

documents.title: Office Visit — Anemia
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
OFFICE VISIT — microcytic anemia

Here to go over the anemia his employer's screening picked up in December. Occupational health started ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily; he has taken it faithfully for six weeks and notices no difference, but he felt fine to begin with. Denies fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, palpitations or shortness of breath. Lifts and runs four days a week and has never felt limited. Bowels regular; no black or bloody stool, no change in consistency.

Diet: mixed, includes meat, grains and vegetables. No alcohol, tobacco or recreational drugs.
FH: asked specifically — his father and a paternal uncle were each told years ago that they had "small red blood cells." Neither needed treatment or a transfusion. Father's AS as previously noted.
Meds: ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily (occupational health). NKDA.

Exam: vitals normal. Well appearing, in no distress. No pallor. No jaundice; sclerae anicteric. Heart regular, no murmur; lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.

Data:
- Workplace CBC 12/7/22 (occ health letter): mild microcytic anemia.
- Repeat CBC 1/12: unchanged microcytic anemia despite a month of iron.
- Iron and ferritin 1/12: normal.
- Hgb electrophoresis 1/12 (resulted 1/19): HbA2 5.4% (elevated), HbF 1.8% (mildly elevated).

Assessment/Plan:
Beta thalassemia minor. Normal iron stores, no response to iron, raised A2 and the paternal history all fit.
- Stop the ferrous sulfate; he isn't iron deficient and extra iron isn't helpful.
- Explained this is a carrier trait he was born with. His hemoglobin will always run a little low with small cells and that's his baseline; it shouldn't be treated with iron unless iron studies are low.
- Carrier counseling: if he plans to have children, a partner can be checked with a CBC and electrophoresis.
- Problem list updated.
No separate follow-up needed. See him for his physical.

documents.title: After your visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Summary from today:
- Your small red cells and slightly low hemoglobin come from beta thalassemia trait (beta thalassemia minor), which you were born with — most likely from your dad's side.
- Stop the iron pills.
- Your blood count will always look a little like this. If another doctor or a screening flags it, tell them about the trait so you aren't put back on iron unnecessarily.
- If you and a future partner plan to have children, a partner can be checked with a simple blood test.
As you asked, I'll send occupational health a short letter with the result.

documents.title: Letter to occupational health
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
To the occupational health clinic,

Re: Min-jun Burgos, DOB 07/05/1996

With the patient's permission: further evaluation of the microcytic anemia found at his 12/07/2022 screening shows beta thalassemia minor (trait), with normal iron studies. Iron supplementation has been stopped. No work restrictions. His blood count will continue to show mild microcytic anemia as his baseline.

Primary Care

documents.title: Office Visit — Low Back Pain
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
OFFICE VISIT — low back pain

27M with beta thalassemia minor (dx Jan 2023), here for back pain he messaged about. Six months of low back pain, started around July. Stiff and sore on waking, eases once he's up and moving, better after a workout. Several stretches of over-the-counter ibuprofen over those months with little benefit. No injury.
He also mentions that a few times over the past year he had a red, sore eye; an eye clinic told him it was mild anterior uveitis, and each episode settled. He doesn't have those records.
No personal skin problems. There is psoriasis in the family — his father.
Never smoker. No alcohol. Works as a software engineer.

Meds: ibuprofen OTC as needed. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vitals unremarkable. Comfortable seated. Eyes white and quiet today. Lumbar forward flexion reduced. Tender to pressure over both sacroiliac joints. Strength and reflexes symmetric in the legs; straight-leg raise negative. Skin: no psoriatic plaques, nails normal.

Results (ordered from his message):
- CRP 1/22: elevated.
- ESR 1/22: elevated.
- HLA-B27: positive.
- SI joint films 1/23: bilateral sacroiliitis.

A/P:
1. Ankylosing spondylitis — inflammatory-pattern back pain, bilateral sacroiliitis, HLA-B27 positive, raised markers, father with AS. Referring to rheumatology to discuss treatment. Reviewed what AS is and why treatment early matters.
2. Recurrent anterior uveitis — by his report; fits with #1. Added to the problem list. Told him an eye that turns red, painful or light-sensitive needs to be seen that day.
3. Beta thalassemia minor — stable trait.
Rheum referral sent today.

documents.title: AS question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thanks for today. I remember my dad being in a lot of pain with his back. Is there anything I should be doing before I see rheumatology? Keep taking the Advil?

documents.title: RE: AS question
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Treatment has come a long way since your dad was diagnosed, and you're being caught early. Until you see rheumatology: keep moving — exercise helps this kind of back pain more than rest — and ibuprofen as needed is fine if it helps at all. Rheumatology will talk through the medicines that actually change the disease. Anything with your eyes, call us that day.

documents.author: rheumatology

OUTSIDE RHEUMATOLOGY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of service: 03/07/2024
Re: Min-jun Burgos, DOB 07/05/1996

Dear Colleague,

Thank you for asking us to see Mr. Burgos for ankylosing spondylitis.

He is 27 with beta thalassemia minor. For about six months he has had low back pain that is at its worst in the morning and improves as he exercises. He describes several brief bouts of mild anterior uveitis over the last year. He has had no recent infections and no abdominal pain, diarrhea or blood in the stool. Ibuprofen has given him little relief.

Medications: none regularly (ibuprofen as needed).
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: father with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriasis.
Social: software engineer; never smoker; no alcohol.

Examination: Tenderness over both sacroiliac joints. Lumbar range of motion reduced in all planes. Modified Schober's test abnormal.

Imaging: Pelvis/SI joint radiographs from 01/23/2024 reviewed — bilateral sacroiliitis.
Labs: HLA-B27 positive; CRP and ESR elevated (01/22/2024).

Impression: Ankylosing spondylitis, active, with recurrent anterior uveitis. Beta thalassemia minor, noted for blood-count monitoring.

Plan:
1. Sulfasalazine, building up over the first month to 1,000 mg twice daily.
2. Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks once screening is back. Requisition given for QuantiFERON and hepatitis B serologies, with a baseline CBC and CMP, to be drawn at your lab.
3. CBC and CMP about a month after starting sulfasalazine, then every three months. Please forward results.
4. Daily back mobility exercises reviewed.
5. Follow-up in one month.

Sincerely,
Rheumatology
